newsitem.title: INDIA: India, Pakistan edge towards renewed dialogue.
newsitem.headline: India, Pakistan edge towards renewed dialogue.

text.p: India and Pakistan, weary of their costly diplomatic standoff, are expected to reopen deadlocked peace talks after prime minister-elect Nawaz Sharif assumes power in Islamabad, analysts and diplomats said.

The longtime foes have reached a critical juncture in their relations, strained by decades of enmity which sprang from the creation of the two nations in the bloody partition of British India in 1947, they said.
Pakistan's elections and Sharif's resounding victory are expected to clear the way for the resumption of high-level talks which reached a dead end in early 1994.

No quick resolution of differences, notably their 50-year struggle over Kashmir, is anticipated. But a blend of factors, some peculiar to Pakistan, others outside its borders, has increased pressure on Islamabad to agree to talks, they said.
"All the factors together argue against a continuation of deadlock and tension," said Bhabani Sengupta, executive director of the Centre for Research on International Change.
"Various elements outside of Pakistan create an environment that is more conducive to talking," a European diplomat said.

Both Sharif and Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda have expressed a desire to resume the high-level dialogue which was suspended in January 1994 when intractable differences over Kashmir, divided between the two neighbours, blocked progress.
Tension between India and Pakistan, both believed capable of assembling nuclear weapons, has cast a nuclear shadow over the entire South Asian region and stirred international concern.

Sengupta said he expected an exchange of messages soon after Sharif assumes power, set for February 17, followed by a meeting of foreign secretaries by mid-March. The last round of bilateral talks in 1994 was headed by the foreign secretaries.
Foreign ministers, senior to secretaries, would then meet.
Why the tempered optimism?

Sharif's win coincides with mounting frustration in Pakistan over both the ailing economy and the standoff with India which has barred any significant rise in bilateral trade. India, meanwhile, has recorded average annual economic growth of seven percent over the past three years.
"Pakistanis realise business with India is for Pakistan's good, that a zero sum game doesn't work," Sengupta said.
Sharif is expected to lend a sympathetic ear to trading interests yearning for closer ties with India.

"His constituency in terms of the industrial and enterpreneurial class there and their desire to open trade links with India are very positive straws in the wind," U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for South Asian Affairs Robin Raphel said.
A major obstacle to renewed negotiations has been Pakistan's longstanding demand that any progress be linked to the resolution of the half-century-old Kashmir dispute.

But Pakistan's efforts to isolate India internationally over Kashmir have foundered, diplomats said. India has ridden out a seven-year-old armed insurgency in the two thirds of the Himalayan region which it controls, they said.

Under a diplomatic offensive called the "Gujral doctrine", named after Foreign Minister Inder Kumar Gujral, India has struck landmark water-sharing pacts with Bangladesh and Nepal, leading to warmer ties and opening new business horizons.
New Delhi's drive to strengthen trade and diplomatic ties with South East Asia could fail unless the threat of conflict in South Asia is reduced, analysts said.
Islamabad is concerned India and Iran could forge an axis to thwart the Taleban militia in Afghanistan, they said.

Once talks were resumed, India and Pakistan could discuss the demilitarisation of the Siachen glacier, where their troops face each other in a frigid standoff. Islamabad could extend Most Favoured Nation trading status to India, diplomats said.
Pakistan's army, still a powerful political actor behind the scenes, has long balked at compromise with India.
"But Sharif's large majority in parliament gives him a stronger hand vis-a-vis the military," a Western diplomat said.
